16.title: The Cold War and the Americas

records.title: Truman: reconversion and the Fair Deal
records.summary: Truman sought to retain the social ambitions of the New Deal while managing demobilisation, inflation and labour conflict. Congressional opposition limited the reach of reform.
evidence: Taft–Hartley Act (1947), passed over Truman’s veto
Fair Deal programme (1949); expansion of Social Security (1950)
records.debate: Distinguish proposals from legislation: limited enactment does not mean no lasting change.
records.recall: Why did conservative opposition constrain the Fair Deal?
questions: To what extent did Truman achieve his domestic reform objectives?
Evaluate the importance of Congress in shaping Truman’s domestic record.

records.title: Eisenhower: Modern Republicanism
records.summary: Eisenhower combined fiscal caution with acceptance of important New Deal institutions. His presidency offers a test of continuity alongside selective federal intervention.
evidence: Department of Health, Education and Welfare (1953)
records.debate: Weigh restrained rhetoric against the actual expansion of federal responsibilities.
records.recall: Identify two continuities with the New Deal and one departure.
questions: How far did Eisenhower change the role of the federal government?
Compare the domestic priorities of Truman and Eisenhower.

records.title: Kennedy and the New Frontier
records.summary: Kennedy’s programme promised renewal but faced a narrow electoral mandate and congressional resistance. Separate policy ambitions, measures enacted in his lifetime and later legislation.
evidence: Civil rights address and proposed legislation (1963)
records.debate: Avoid crediting Kennedy with Johnson’s legislative achievements without explaining the connection.
records.recall: Which reforms were proposals rather than laws before November 1963?
questions: Assess the domestic achievements of Kennedy’s presidency.
To what extent was congressional opposition responsible for the limitations of the New Frontier?

records.title: Johnson and the Great Society
records.summary: Johnson used legislative experience and the 1964 electoral victory to extend social reform. Legal gains and poverty programmes coexisted with urban unrest and the costs of Vietnam.
records.debate: Judge success using separate criteria for legal equality, poverty and durable social change.
records.recall: Explain why legislative success did not remove economic inequality.
questions: Evaluate the success of Johnson’s Great Society.
Compare the domestic achievements of Kennedy and Johnson.

records.title: Nixon: domestic policy and the economy
records.summary: Nixon mixed conservative electoral appeals with pragmatic federal intervention. Economic instability and social conflict complicate a simple picture of a uniformly conservative administration.
evidence: End of dollar convertibility into gold (1971)
records.debate: Assess policy by its effects as well as its ideological label.
records.recall: How did intervention in the economy sit alongside conservative rhetoric?
questions: How far were Nixon’s domestic policies conservative?
Evaluate Nixon’s response to the economic problems facing the United States.

records.title: Watergate and presidential accountability
records.summary: The break-in became a constitutional crisis through the cover-up, investigations and conflict over presidential evidence. Nixon resigned before the full House voted on impeachment.
evidence: House Judiciary Committee impeachment articles; resignation (August 1974)
records.debate: Distinguish the original break-in from abuse of power and the cover-up.
records.recall: Why is it inaccurate to say Nixon was impeached and removed?
questions: Evaluate the consequences of Watergate for the presidency.
Assess the role of constitutional checks in bringing about Nixon’s resignation.

records.title: Ford and Carter: trust and stagflation
records.summary: Ford and Carter faced damaged public confidence and difficult economic conditions. Their records invite comparison between leadership choices and structural constraints.
records.debate: Do not explain economic performance solely through presidential competence.
records.recall: What political costs and possible benefits followed Ford’s pardon?
questions: Compare Ford’s and Carter’s responses to domestic economic problems.
To what extent did Carter restore confidence in federal government?

records.title: Party conflict and electoral change
records.summary: Civil rights, Vietnam and social change fractured existing party coalitions. Electoral victories reflected changing alliances as well as candidates and immediate events.
records.debate: Separate short-term electoral shocks from a longer realignment of voters and regions.
records.recall: How did civil rights policy affect party coalitions?
questions: Assess the impact of internal party divisions on US elections in the 1960s and 1970s.
How important was social change in reshaping Republican and Democratic support?

records.title: St Laurent and Diefenbaker
records.summary: Post-war Canadian governments balanced development, welfare, national identity and relations with the United States. Compare the priorities of Liberal and Progressive Conservative leadership.
evidence: Federal voting rights extended to status First Nations people without loss of status (1960)
records.debate: Distinguish the 1960 statutory Bill of Rights from the constitutional Charter of 1982.
records.recall: How far did economic development strengthen political stability?
questions: Compare the domestic policies of St Laurent and Diefenbaker.
Evaluate Diefenbaker’s contribution to political and social change in Canada.

records.title: Pearson and Trudeau: reform and nationhood
records.summary: Reform extended social provision and reshaped federal identity, while debates over bilingualism, rights and Quebec challenged national unity. The syllabus extends Canada to 1982.
evidence: Constitution Act and Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982)
records.debate: Assess inclusion and national cohesion separately; reform could also deepen disagreements.
records.recall: Why did bilingualism matter to Trudeau’s vision of Canada?
questions: Evaluate the domestic achievements of Pearson and Trudeau.
How far did Trudeau strengthen Canadian national unity by 1982?

records.title: Quiet Revolution and Quebec nationalism
records.summary: Secularisation, state-led modernisation and greater Francophone confidence transformed Quebec. Constitutional nationalism and the FLQ’s violence pursued different paths.
records.debate: Avoid treating all Quebec nationalists as separatists or supporters of violence.
records.recall: How did economic and cultural change reinforce nationalism?
questions: Analyse the causes of the Quiet Revolution.
Evaluate the impact of Quebec nationalism on Canada up to 1980.

records.title: October Crisis: security and liberty
records.summary: FLQ kidnappings provoked an exceptional federal response. The crisis raises questions about public protection, civil liberties and the political consequences of coercion.
evidence: Kidnappings of James Cross and Pierre Laporte
Arrests and subsequent debate over emergency powers
records.debate: Differentiate the immediate security outcome from the wider consequences for rights and nationalism.
records.recall: What evidence could support and challenge Trudeau’s response?
questions: Assess the consequences of the October Crisis for Canada.
To what extent was Trudeau’s handling of the October Crisis justified by its outcomes?

records.title: Truman: containment in the hemisphere
records.summary: US policy prioritised the prevention of communist influence. Latin American demands for development and sovereign equality could conflict with Washington’s focus on security.
evidence: Unequal priorities over aid and defence
records.debate: Distinguish the stated defence of freedom from support for anti-communist stability.
records.recall: Why could Latin American governments resent containment?
questions: Evaluate the impact of Truman’s containment policy on the Americas.
How far did security concerns outweigh economic development in US policy towards Latin America?

records.title: McCarthyism and the Red Scare
records.summary: Anti-communism shaped employment, culture and political debate. McCarthy was one actor within a broader climate involving executive action, congressional investigations and public anxiety.
records.debate: Do not attribute every loyalty investigation or blacklist to McCarthy personally.
records.recall: How did fear of communism affect free expression?
questions: Assess the social and cultural effects of McCarthyism.
Evaluate the influence of anti-communism on US domestic and foreign policy.

records.title: Korea: participation and consequences
records.summary: The Korean War internationalised containment through a UN intervention. Study changes in military aims and the consequences for US and Canadian policy.
records.debate: Separate the defence of South Korea from the later attempt to reunify Korea by force.
records.recall: Why did the war become a limited conflict rather than a decisive victory?
questions: Evaluate the reasons for US participation in the Korean War.
Assess the political and diplomatic consequences of the Korean War for the Americas.

records.title: Eisenhower and Dulles: the New Look
records.summary: The New Look sought to contain communism while controlling costs through nuclear deterrence, alliances and covert action. Regional outcomes could undermine democratic commitments.
records.debate: Measure success through both immediate strategic goals and longer-term legitimacy.
records.recall: Why did covert action appeal to Eisenhower?
questions: Evaluate the impact of the New Look on Latin America.
How successful was Eisenhower’s foreign policy in protecting US interests in the Americas?

records.title: Kennedy: Cuba and the Alliance for Progress
records.summary: Kennedy combined development aid with determined opposition to communist influence. Cuba exposed the limits of intervention and the dangers of superpower confrontation.
records.debate: Distinguish crisis management from the long-term success of development policies.
records.recall: Why could reform and intervention work against each other?
questions: Assess the achievements of Kennedy’s Alliance for Progress.
To what extent did Kennedy improve US relations with Latin America?

records.title: Vietnam: reasons and stages of involvement
records.summary: US involvement moved from assistance and advisers to large-scale war, then Vietnamisation and withdrawal. Explain decisions in the context of containment, credibility and perceived local weakness.
evidence: Support for France and then South Vietnam
records.debate: Avoid treating escalation as an inevitable or unchanging policy.
records.recall: How did the reasons for involvement change between presidents?
questions: Analyse the reasons for the escalation of US involvement in Vietnam.
Compare the approaches of Johnson and Nixon to the Vietnam War.

records.title: Vietnam: domestic opposition and the end
records.summary: War costs, casualties, conscription and the credibility gap weakened support. Withdrawal and the later fall of South Vietnam need distinct explanations.
records.debate: Weigh protest against military, diplomatic and electoral pressures rather than assuming one cause.
records.recall: Why are 1973 and 1975 both important dates?
questions: Evaluate the domestic impact of the Vietnam War on the United States.
How important was opposition at home in ending US military involvement in Vietnam?

records.title: Vietnam: Canadian and Latin American responses
records.summary: Responses outside the US complicate a simple picture of hemispheric solidarity. Canada’s refusal to send combat forces coexisted with close economic and strategic ties.
evidence: Canadian trade and defence connections with the US
records.debate: Distinguish official policy, economic relationships and popular opposition.
records.recall: Why is Canadian non-participation different from complete disengagement?
questions: Assess Canada’s response to the Vietnam War.
Evaluate the significance of opposition to the Vietnam War elsewhere in the Americas.

records.title: Nixon: Chile and covert intervention
records.summary: Washington sought to undermine Allende, but Chilean actors and domestic conflict were also crucial. Explain external pressure without erasing local agency.
records.debate: Distinguish evidence of US destabilisation from an unsupported claim that the US directly controlled every action in the coup.
records.recall: How would you weigh external pressure against domestic causes?
questions: Evaluate the impact of Nixon’s policies towards Chile.
To what extent did Cold War priorities shape US intervention in Latin America?

records.title: Carter: human rights and Panama
records.summary: Carter foregrounded human rights and renegotiated control of the Panama Canal. Strategic considerations and inconsistent application limited the coherence of his approach.
records.debate: Assess the difference between a declared principle and its implementation.
records.recall: Why did the Panama treaties matter for regional relations?
questions: Evaluate Carter’s human-rights policy in the Americas.
Compare the priorities of Nixon and Carter in Latin America.

records.title: Case study: Canada in the Cold War
records.summary: Canada pursued collective defence alongside diplomacy and a measure of autonomy. Link foreign-policy choices to domestic politics and public debate.
records.debate: Avoid assuming that alliance membership eliminated independent Canadian choices.
records.recall: How did Canada balance cooperation with the US and independent diplomacy?
questions: Evaluate the effects of the Cold War on Canadian foreign policy.
Assess the relationship between Cold War security and domestic politics in Canada.

records.title: Case study workshop: one non-US country
records.summary: The syllabus requires a non-US case study. Canada is developed here; another country can be used if studied in comparable depth and agreed with your teacher.
evidence: Assess effects on government, economy and society
records.debate: A few references to Cuba or Chile are not a substitute for a coherent national case study.
records.recall: Can you build a timeline linking external pressures and internal policy?
questions: How far did Cold War pressures determine the policies of one country of the Americas other than the USA?
Evaluate the domestic impact of the Cold War in one non-US country of the Americas.

records.title: Indigenous rights: Canada
records.summary: Indigenous campaigns challenged assimilation and demanded recognition, land rights and political voice. Treat First Nations, Inuit and Métis experiences with care rather than as a single uniform story.
records.debate: Legal recognition and substantive self-determination are different measures of progress.
records.recall: Why did many Indigenous leaders oppose the 1969 White Paper?
questions: Evaluate the achievements of Indigenous rights movements in Canada.
How far did government policy advance Indigenous rights in post-war Canada?

records.title: Indigenous rights: wider Americas
records.summary: Campaigns for land, cultural recognition and autonomy took different forms across the region. Compare specific communities and states, using precise evidence.
evidence: Land and recognition campaigns in Latin America
records.debate: Avoid projecting US protest tactics onto all Indigenous movements.
records.recall: How did land and sovereignty distinguish these campaigns from other rights movements?
questions: Compare the challenges faced by Indigenous rights movements in two countries of the Americas.
Assess the effectiveness of protest in advancing Indigenous rights.

records.title: Origins, litigation and school desegregation
records.summary: Legal activism built on long-standing organising against segregation. Supreme Court decisions created opportunities, but local resistance made implementation uneven.
records.debate: Separate the legal destruction of segregation from the pace of actual integration.
records.recall: Why did Brown require enforcement beyond the courtroom?
questions: Evaluate the role of the Supreme Court in advancing African American civil rights.
Analyse the origins of the post-war African American civil rights movement.

records.title: Grassroots action and civil rights organisations
records.summary: Boycotts, sit-ins, freedom rides and voter registration widened participation. Organisations differed over priorities and methods while interacting with federal politics.
records.debate: Compare the contributions of local activists, SNCC, CORE, SCLC and NAACP instead of writing a single-leader narrative.
records.recall: How did direct action place pressure on national government?
questions: Assess the effectiveness of non-violent direct action in the civil rights movement.
How important were grassroots organisations in securing civil rights gains?

records.title: Martin Luther King Jr: leadership and limits
records.summary: King connected moral leadership, organisation and publicity with specific campaigns. His widening focus on economic justice and Vietnam also exposed tensions within the movement.
records.debate: Assess leadership in relation to activists, opponents and federal action rather than in isolation.
records.recall: Which achievements depended on King, and which had broader causes?
questions: Evaluate King’s contribution to African American civil rights.
To what extent was national leadership the main cause of civil rights progress?

records.title: Malcolm X, Black Power and the Panthers
records.summary: Radical activism questioned the pace and goals of integration. Nationalism, self-defence and community programmes were distinct ideas whose development should not be collapsed together.
evidence: Malcolm X’s evolving position before his death (1965)
records.debate: Malcolm X died before the 1966 popularisation of Black Power; influence is different from organisational leadership.
records.recall: How did aims and methods differ between Malcolm X and the Panthers?
questions: Analyse the reasons for the growth of radical African American activism.
Evaluate the impact of Black Power on the civil rights movement.

records.title: Government action and the limits of equality
records.summary: Courts, presidents and Congress enabled important gains but also reflected political calculation and resistance. Assess legal, political and socioeconomic outcomes separately.
evidence: Continuing inequality and resistance to school integration
records.debate: A change in law is necessary evidence of progress, but not proof of equal outcomes.
records.recall: How could the federal government both assist and restrict change?
questions: Evaluate the role of the federal government in advancing African American civil rights.
How far had the civil rights movement achieved its aims by 1980?

records.title: Feminism: United States
records.summary: Second-wave feminism challenged legal discrimination, employment barriers and assumptions about family roles. Class, race and ideological divisions shaped experiences and priorities.
evidence: Roe v. Wade (1973); ERA ratification campaign
records.debate: Assess achievements within the period; do not present a failed constitutional amendment as enacted law.
records.recall: What differed between legal reform and changing everyday expectations?
questions: Analyse the reasons for the growth of feminism in the United States.
Evaluate the achievements and limitations of US feminist movements by 1980.

records.title: Feminism: Canada and regional comparison
records.summary: Canadian campaigns connected employment, political representation and family policy. Compare national institutional opportunities while recognising diversity within movements.
evidence: Royal Commission on the Status of Women established (1967)
records.debate: Avoid using one country as a proxy for the whole Americas; match the dates required by the question.
records.recall: Why did government commissions offer both opportunities and limits?
questions: Compare the achievements of feminist movements in two countries of the Americas.
Evaluate the impact of feminism on Canadian society.

records.title: Hispanic American movement and labour rights
records.summary: Labour organising, cultural affirmation and political participation challenged exclusion. Chavez and Huerta linked workplace demands to broader campaigns for dignity and rights.
records.debate: The 1965 merger announcement and the 1966 union formation are sometimes dated differently; distinguish organisational stages.
records.recall: How did a consumer boycott increase workers’ bargaining power?
questions: Evaluate Cesar Chavez’s contribution to Hispanic American rights.
Assess the effectiveness of the methods used by the Hispanic American movement.

records.title: Immigration reform and Hispanic communities
records.summary: Immigration law and labour movements overlapped without being identical. Policy changes affected opportunities and restrictions differently across groups.
evidence: Continuing debates over migrant labour and status
records.debate: Do not assume that reform removed all restrictions or benefited every Hispanic community equally.
records.recall: How did immigration policy interact with labour rights?
questions: Evaluate the significance of immigration reform for Hispanic Americans.
How far did government policy meet the demands of Hispanic American movements?

records.title: Youth culture, protest and counterculture
records.summary: Youth activism challenged war, authority and social conventions. Political organising and countercultural lifestyles overlapped but did not represent all young people.
evidence: Mexico City student movement and Tlatelolco repression (1968)
Anti-war protests and alternative cultural practices
records.debate: Compare political demands, cultural expression and government responses rather than assuming a unified youth movement.
records.recall: How did youth protest differ between the US and Mexico?
questions: Evaluate the impact of youth protest in the Americas.
To what extent did counterculture transform society in the 1960s and 1970s?
